identity.title: ALMA-IMF: XV. Core mass function in the high-mass star formation regime

paper_type_evidence.quote: The goal of the ALMA-IMF large program is to measure the core mass function at high linear resolution (2700 au) in 15 typical Milky Way protoclusters spanning a mass range of 2.5×10 [3] to 32.7×10 [3] _M_ ⊙ .
The data were taken from the ALMA-IMF large program (Project ID: 2017.1.01355.L), entitled _ALMA_ _transforms_ _our_ _view of the origin of stellar masses_ .

question.value: Measure the core mass function (CMF) at a homogeneous physical resolution of 2700 au across 15 Milky Way high-mass protoclusters and test whether its high-mass slope differs from the canonical Salpeter IMF slope (α = 2.35).

evidence.quote: The goal of the ALMA-IMF large program is to measure the core mass function at high linear resolution (2700 au) in 15 typical Milky Way protoclusters spanning a mass range of 2.5×10 [3] to 32.7×10 [3] _M_ ⊙ .
The ALMA-IMF large program aims to test if the high-mass slope of the CMF differs from the high-mass slope of the canonical IMF (α = 2.35 when fitted by a power-law, Salpeter 1955).
The data were taken from the ALMA-IMF large program (Project ID: 2017.1.01355.L), entitled _ALMA_ _transforms_ _our_ _view of the origin of stellar masses_ .
This paper makes use of the following ALMA data: ADS/JAO.ALMA#2017.1.01355.L.
This paper also use the following ALMA data: ADS/JAO. ALMA#2013.1.01365.S and ADS/JAO.ALMA#2015.1.01273.S.

analysis_steps.goal: Extract compact continuum sources and compare algorithms

method.value: Two-step extraction on both native and 2700 au smoothed maps using getsf and GExt2D: detect source candidates on 1.3 mm maps without primary beam correction, then measure fluxes and sizes on 1.3 mm and 3 mm maps after primary beam correction.

evidence.quote: To extract sources in the continuum emission maps, we used two extraction tools: _getsf_ (v210414, Men’shchikov 2021b) and _GExt2D_ (v210603, Bontemps et al., in prep.).

evidence.loc: 3.2. Source extraction at native angular resolutions

fitting.value: Automated Gaussian fitting after background subtraction in GExt2D; multi-scale decomposition in getsf; linear regression on complementary cumulative source flux functions (SFFs) above the 12 mJy median.

evidence.quote: The third step corresponds to automated Gaussian fitting at each locations of compact sources after subtracting the derived background.
We fit the cumulative SFF with a power law from the median value of the samples, that is 12 mJy, up to the flux at which the number of cores is below ten

validation.value: Compared getsf (677 sources) and GExt2D (1020 sources): ~80% of getsf sources are found by GExt2D, both yield identical high-flux SFF slopes (ζ ≃ 1.85), and ~95% of smoothed getsf sources match native-resolution getsf sources.

evidence.quote: We see a good agreement between these extractions as ∼80 % of the sources found by _getsf_ are also found by _GExt2D_ (Table 2).

The fitted highflux slopes are similar for both catalogues, with ζ [′] ≃ 0.85. These exponents, adjusted onto the complementary cumulative SFFs, correspond to power-laws with exponents ζ = ζ [′] + 1 ≃ 1.85.
Indeed, ≃95% of the sources extracted in the smoothed maps were also extracted at the native angular resolutions with the _getsf_ algorithm.

analysis_steps.goal: Filter out free-free contaminated sources using 1.3 mm and 3 mm spectral indices

method.value: Rescale 3 mm integrated fluxes for 1.3 mm vs 3 mm source size differences, compute spectral index γ (Eq. 2), and reject sources with γ < 2. For sources undetected by getsf at 3 mm but lying on pixel-by-pixel spectral index map regions with γ < 2 (3 mm background > 3σ), measure aperture upper-limit 3 mm flux (Eq. 3) and reject those with γ < 1.

evidence.quote: We remove 68 sources with γ < 2, which are presumably contaminated by freefree emission.
For the sources undetected at 3 mm we estimate their flux, _S_ 3 mm [upper] [, using] the integrated flux in the aperture corresponding to the footprint of the source detected at 1.3 mm.
and we rejected the 16 sources with spectral index below 1, those for which free-free emissions could substantially contribute to the emission.

key_parameters.value: Rejection thresholds: γ < 2 for sources detected at 3 mm (68 rejected); γ < 1 for 3 mm aperture upper limits on free-free background (16 rejected).

evidence.quote: We remove 68 sources with γ < 2, which are presumably contaminated by freefree emission.
and we rejected the 16 sources with spectral index below 1, those for which free-free emissions could substantially contribute to the emission.

evidence.quote: This rescaling works both for an optically thick emission and for an optically thin emission of an isothermal protostellar envelope with a density profile ρ( _r_ ) ∝ _r_ [−][2], where _r_ is the radius of the envelope.

validation.value: Visual inspection of sources overlaid on pixel-by-pixel spectral index maps where 3 mm intensity exceeds 3σ.

evidence.quote: The maps display the spectral index value only where the 3 mm intensity exceeds 3 σ.

analysis_steps.goal: Assign dust temperatures to each core

method.value: Assign per-core dust temperatures from 2.5" resolution PPMAP Bayesian SED fitting maps (combining free-free decontaminated ALMA Band 6, SOFIA/HAWC+, Herschel PACS/SPIRE, and APEX SABOCA/LABOCA), overriding with 100±50 K for 49 methyl formate hot core candidates and 300±100 K for 3 extreme hot cores.

evidence.quote: Following the pilot study by Motte et al. (2018), we used the Bayesian procedure _PPMAP_ (Marsh et al. 2015; Dell’Ova et al. 2024) to build the temperature maps of the ALMA-IMF protoclusters.

Following the method discussed in Bonfand et al. (2024), we set 100±50 K to the 49 sources whose position corresponds to the peaks of extended methyl formate emission; these sources are classified as hot core candidates.
Additionally, we set 300±100 K to sources n [◦] 1, n [◦] 2, and n [◦] 1 in W51-IRS2, W51-E and G327.29 respectively

key_parameters.value: PPMAP angular resolution = 2.5"; temperature uncertainty = 25% (or 5 K for T < 20 K); hot core T = 100±50 K or 300±100 K.

evidence.quote: Finally, we obtain a unique temperature for each ′′ core at an angular resolution of 2.5 .
The error associated with _PPMAP_ derivation is ≈5 K; to account for potential systematic contributions, we adopt a 25% error on the _PPMAP_ temperature estimates [5] .

assumptions.value: Methyl formate (CH3OCHO) sublimates from dust grains at ~100 K and traces internal heating in hot cores.

evidence.quote: Methyl formate forms at the surface of dust grains in lukewarm (30-40 K) regions, and is then released in the gas phase when the temperature reaches ∼100 K (e.g. Garrod et al. 2009).

fitting.value: Bayesian procedure PPMAP (detailed in Dell'Ova et al. 2024)

evidence.quote: Following the pilot study by Motte et al. (2018), we used the Bayesian procedure _PPMAP_ (Marsh et al. 2015; Dell’Ova et al. 2024) to build the temperature maps of the ALMA-IMF protoclusters.

analysis_steps.goal: Derive core masses and evaluate gravitational boundedness

method.value: Convert 1.3 mm integrated and peak fluxes to core mass using Eq. 4 (with first-order optical depth correction), and evaluate gravitational boundedness using the critical Bonnor-Ebert mass ratio M_BE / M_core < 2.

evidence.quote: We converted the measured integrated flux at 1.3 mm, _S_ 1 [int] .3 mm [,] into a mass using the formula presented in Paper III that includes a first order correction for the optical thickness
We consider that the sources are gravitationally bound if _M_ BE / _M_ source < 2 (see e.g. Louvet et al. 2021). As listed in Table 3, this filter excludes no sources.

key_parameters.value: Boundedness threshold: M_BE / M_source < 2; M_BE = 2.4 * R * σ_th^2 / G; R = (a * b^2)^(1/3) * D.

evidence.quote: where _M_ core is the core mass and _M_ BE is the mass of the critical Bonnor-Ebert sphere (Bonnor 1956) whose size matches that of the core: _M_ BE = 2.4 × _R_ × σ [2] th [/] _[G]_ [.]
We consider that the sources are gravitationally bound if _M_ BE / _M_ source < 2 (see e.g. Louvet et al. 2021).

assumptions.value: Dust + gas opacity per unit mass κ_1.3mm = 0.1 * (ν / 1000 GHz)^β cm^2 g^-1 with β = 1.5 (Ossenkopf & Henning 1994); isothermal adiabatic index γ = 1; mean molecular weight per free particle µ = 2.4.

evidence.quote: κ 1.3 mm = 0.1 (ν/1000 GHz) [β] cm [2] g [−][1] is the dust opacity per unit mass (dust + gas), with an opacity index β = 1.5 typical of cold and dense environment (Ossenkopf & Henning 1994)
where γ = 1 is the adiabatic index (isothermal), _k_ _B_ is the Boltzmann constant, µ = 2.4 is the mean molecular weight per free particle, and _m_ p is the mass of a proton.

validation.value: Checked that assuming a 3D oblate core shape (V ∝ a^2 * b) instead of prolate (V ∝ a * b^2) has no effect on core boundedness.

evidence.quote: We stress that choosing 3D oblate core shape ( _V_ ∝ _a_ 2 × _b_ ) has no effect on the boundedness of the cores.

analysis_steps.goal: Determine mass completeness limits per field via synthetic core injection

method.value: Inject synthetic 2D circular Gaussian cores (FWHM = 3840 au) onto the source-subtracted background maps in 10 mass bins across 4 draws (~3800 synthetic cores per field), re-extract with getsf, and find the 90% recovery mass limit.

evidence.quote: we injected synthetic cores on top of their background emission (i.e. the emission subtracted from each source). The synthetic cores are injected in the form of 2D circular Gaussian with a FWHM corresponding to 3840 au
We then extract the synthetic cores with the _getsf_ method (see Sect. 3.1). To obtain a good statistics in each bin of mass, we repeated this procedure four times per field.
We define the completeness as the mass limit above which more than 90 % of the synthetic cores get extracted.

key_parameters.value: Gaussian FWHM = 3840 au; minimum separation > 2.5"; border exclusion = 5"; 10 flux bins (equivalent to 0.5-5 M_sun at 20 K, or 1-10 M_sun in W51-E); 4 draws per field (~3800 cores total); completeness threshold = 90%.

evidence.quote: We inject these synthetic sources randomly, provided the centre of the cores are separated by more than 2.5 [′′] . We forbid the injection of sources within 5 [′′] of the border of the maps
The flux of the synthetic sources ranges from equivalent masses of 0.5 to 5 _M_ ⊙ in all fields for gas at 20 K, except in W51-E where we adopted a mass range of 1 to 10 _M_ ⊙ .
Cumulating the four draws we obtain ≃3800 cores in total in each field (or ≃380 per bin) and we probe ≃80 % of the background area.

assumptions.value: Synthetic core fluxes converted to mass using the mean temperature of the cores extracted in the corresponding region.

evidence.quote: From these fluxes, we compute the mass of the synthetic cores when adopting the mean temperature of the cores extracted in the corresponding region.

validation.value: Discarded W51-E (completeness limit 3.86 M_sun) and adopted the highest remaining field completeness limit (1.64 M_sun) as the global completeness limit.

evidence.quote: We exclude W51-E from the analysis of the global CMF (see Sect. 6.1) and we restrict the core samples to cores exceeding 1.64 _M_ ⊙ to fit the high-mass tail of the CMF.

analysis_steps.goal: Fit the high-mass slope of the global CMF and quantify uncertainties and Salpeter tension

method.value: Fit a power-law PDF p(x) ∝ x^-α to the 330 bound cores above x_min = 1.64 M_sun (excluding W51-E) using Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance in the powerlaw Python package, propagate uncertainties via 10^3 Monte Carlo realizations, and test tension with Salpeter (α = 2.35) via 10^5 synthetic draws.

evidence.quote: We follow the procedure presented by Clauset et al. (2009), and use its implementation in the python package `powerlaw` presented by Alstott et al. (2014).
We show the resulting cumulative CMFs generated from 10 [3] trials in Fig. 6. Each draw is fitted via MLE (see Sect. 5.2.1), fixing _x_ min to 1.64 _M_ ⊙ .
we selected 330 sources from a perfect mass distribution with an exponent of 2.35 and fitted the slope of its high-mass tail through the MLE. We repeated the operation 10 [5] times.

key_parameters.value: x_min = 1.64 M_sun; n = 330 cores; 10^3 Monte Carlo trials with β ~ N(1.5, 0.2), T ~ N(T_core, σ_T), and Gaussian flux errors; 10^5 Salpeter synthetic trials.

evidence.quote: We confirm that the CMF in a representative sample of high-mass Galactic protoclusters is shallower than the Salpeter slope. We suggest that these massive protoclusters will give birth to top-heavy stellar clusters, or, in order to reconcile with the Universal IMF, the CMF needs to evolve and become Salpeterlike at latter stages of the cluster formation.

claims.hypothesis: Mean extracted core sizes depend on the linear physical resolution of the observations.
claims.experiment: Extracted sources from the 15 ALMA-IMF Band 6 maps at native resolution (1365 to 2685 au) and again after smoothing all maps with a Gaussian kernel to a matched 2700 au resolution.
claims.result: At native resolution, mean source size increases linearly with physical scale (Fig. 1 left); after smoothing to 2700 au, the mean core size is uniform across all 15 fields at L = 3840 ± 270 au (Fig. 1 right).
claims.finding: Smoothing to a matched physical resolution is required and successfully produces a spatially homogeneous core sample.

evidence.loc: 3.2. Source extraction at native angular resolutions

claims.hypothesis: The statistical properties of the extracted source fluxes are robust against the choice of source extraction algorithm.
claims.experiment: Extracted sources across all 15 smoothed fields using both getsf (677 sources) and GExt2D (1020 sources) and fitted power laws to their complementary cumulative source flux functions (SFFs) above the 12 mJy median.
claims.result: ~80% of getsf sources are recovered by GExt2D, both catalogs have a median flux of ~12 mJy, and both yield an identical high-flux power-law slope of ζ ≃ 1.85 (ζ' ≃ 0.85).
claims.finding: The overall statistics of source flux are independent of the two extraction algorithms employed.

evidence.quote: We see a good agreement between these extractions as ∼80 % of the sources found by _getsf_ are also found by _GExt2D_ (Table 2).

The fitted highflux slopes are similar for both catalogues, with ζ [′] ≃ 0.85. These exponents, adjusted onto the complementary cumulative SFFs, correspond to power-laws with exponents ζ = ζ [′] + 1 ≃ 1.85.
This analysis proves that the overall statistics of source flux is independent of the two extraction algorithms we employed.

claims.hypothesis: The high-mass slope of the core mass function (CMF) in high-mass Galactic protoclusters differs from the canonical Salpeter IMF slope (α = 2.35).
claims.experiment: Derived per-core temperatures (PPMAP and CH3OCHO hot core proxies) and optically-depth-corrected masses for free-free-filtered bound cores across 14 protoclusters above the 1.64 M_sun completeness limit (330 cores), fitted the CMF via Maximum Likelihood Estimation with 10^3 Monte Carlo error trials, and compared against 10^5 synthetic draws of 330 cores from a Salpeter (α = 2.35) distribution.
claims.result: The global CMF above 1.64 M_sun has a power-law slope of α = 1.97 ± 0.06, and the probability of drawing such a slope from a parent Salpeter (α = 2.35) distribution with 330 cores is < 1% (2.4σ).
claims.finding: The CMF in high-mass protoclusters is top-heavy (flatter than Salpeter at the 2.4σ level), implying either atypical top-heavy IMFs under self-similar mapping or subsequent evolution of the CMF toward a Salpeter slope.

evidence.quote: A power-law fit to the CMF of the sub-sample of cores above the 1.64 _M_ ⊙ completeness limit — 330 cores — through the maximum likelihood estimate technique yields a slope of 1.97 ± 0.06, significantly flatter than the 2.35 Salpeter slope.

With 330 cores, the probability of retrieving a slope compatible with ALMA-IMF, α = 1.97 ± 0.06, is lower than 1% (σ ≈ 2.4). Therefore, we report that the CMF in the protoclusters studied by ALMA-IMF is flatter than, and cannot reasonably be reconciled with the Salpeter-IMF slope to a 2.4σ level [9] .

why_this_data.value: Previous CMF studies in high-mass protoclusters used narrow single-pointing fields or disparate physical resolutions and sensitivities; ALMA-IMF observed 15 representative Milky Way high-mass protoclusters (>500 M_sun in inner parts, distances 2-6 kpc) homogeneously at ~2 kau resolution and <60 mK sensitivity at 1.3 mm.

evidence.quote: However, the comparison of core samples between these studies — which are captured at different evolutionary stages — becomes complex or impossible when the observations are carried out at disparate physical resolutions and/or sensitivities. Thus, it became imperative to obtain a sample of high-mass protoclusters representative of the Milky Way observed homogeneously.

why_this_method.value: Used cleanest continuum maps to avoid molecular line contamination; smoothed maps to 2700 au to eliminate resolution bias on core sizes and masses; used two extraction tools (getsf and GExt2D) to test algorithmic bias and selected getsf as more conservative and consistent across resolutions; used Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) instead of binned histograms or cumulative linear regression to avoid binning bias and correlated errors.

evidence.quote: The cleanest maps were constructed flagging all channels contaminated by molecular emission (see Fig. 3 in Paper II). Since we wish to assemble the most reliable sample of cores, we use the cleanest continuum maps

In the following, we choose to focus on the extractions performed by _getsf_ since it is more conservative than _GExt2D_, which is confirmed by the large fraction of _getsf_ sources confirmed with _GExt2D_ .
The representation of a distribution in the form of histograms, as in Fig. 3, further fitted through linear regression may give inaccurate results (Clauset et al. 2009).

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: bsens continuum maps (constructed using the full continuum bandwidth) were rejected in favor of cleanest continuum maps because bsens may include significant molecular line contamination toward hot cores.

evidence.quote: The bsens maps were constructed using the full range of the continuum spectral windows — which may include significant molecular emission, especially toward hot cores. The cleanest maps were constructed flagging all channels contaminated by molecular emission (see Fig. 3 in Paper II). Since we wish to assemble the most reliable sample of cores, we use the cleanest continuum maps

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: GExt2D source catalog was used for comparison but not selected for the main CMF analysis because getsf is more conservative and shows better consistency (95% vs 75%) between native and smoothed resolutions.

evidence.quote: In the following, we choose to focus on the extractions performed by _getsf_ since it is more conservative than _GExt2D_, which is confirmed by the large fraction of _getsf_ sources confirmed with _GExt2D_ .

Indeed, ≃95% of the sources extracted in the smoothed maps were also extracted at the native angular resolutions with the _getsf_ algorithm. This fraction drops to ≃75% in the case of the _GExt2D_ extractions.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: 3D oblate core geometry (V ∝ a^2 * b) was tested as an alternative to prolate geometry (V ∝ a * b^2) and found to have no effect on core boundedness.

evidence.quote: We stress that choosing 3D oblate core shape ( _V_ ∝ _a_ 2 × _b_ ) has no effect on the boundedness of the cores.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: W51-E was excluded from the global CMF fit because its 90% mass completeness limit (3.86 M_sun) is much higher than the other 14 fields (≤ 1.64 M_sun).

evidence.quote: These numbers exclude W51-E, for which we find completeness as high as 3.9 _M_ ⊙ . We exclude W51-E from the analysis of the global CMF (see Sect. 6.1)

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Linear regression on binned histograms or cumulative CMFs was rejected in favor of Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) because histograms suffer from non-Gaussian log-scale noise and arbitrary bin widths, while cumulative distributions have non-independent data points.

evidence.quote: The representation of a distribution in the form of histograms, as in Fig. 3, further fitted through linear regression may give inaccurate results (Clauset et al. 2009).

The representation in the form of a cumulative CMF, however, prevents the estimation of the uncertainty as the data are not independent. To circumvent these issues, we choose to fit the high-mass end of the CMF using maximum likelihood estimates (MLE).

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Exponential and log-normal functional forms were also fitted to the 10^3 Monte Carlo CMF realizations in Appendix E alongside the power-law fit.

how_they_decided_enough.value: Injected ~3800 synthetic cores across 4 draws per field to cover ~80% of the background area for completeness; verified that the 330-core sample above 1.64 M_sun far exceeds the ~40-50 core threshold required for stable MLE power-law index convergence and ran 10^5 Monte Carlo draws to test statistical power against the Salpeter slope.

evidence.quote: Cumulating the four draws we obtain ≃3800 cores in total in each field (or ≃380 per bin) and we probe ≃80 % of the background area.

We put forward that 330 cores above the completeness limit convey a statistical conclusive sample. Clauset et al. (2009) report stable index values when the sample exceeds ≈50 elements above the completeness limits.

limitations_admitted.value: Gravitational boundedness is only a first-order thermal Bonnor-Ebert check because turbulence, external pressure, and magnetic field support are not currently available for each core.

evidence.quote: We note that this is a first-order check of the boundedness of cores. A more accurate determination would require computing the equilibrium of each source taking into account its turbulence, external pressure, and magnetic field support in addition to the thermal support. Unfortunately, we lack all these pieces of information at the moment.

limitations_admitted.value: 84 sources potentially contaminated by free-free emission were rejected rather than flux-corrected and retained (though re-introducing massive free-free-corrected cores would not alter the conclusion).

evidence.quote: Free-free emission: in Sect. 4.2, we rejected all sources that are arguably contaminated by free-free emission from our core sample. We ended up rejecting 84 sources (see Table 3).

limitations_admitted.value: Cores are probed at 2700 au spatial resolution, leaving potential sub-fragmentation and multiplicity on scales below 1000 au (down to ~200 au disk scales) unresolved.

evidence.quote: Sub-fragmentation: we probed the cores at a spatial resolution of 2700 au. Recent observations in the high-mass protostellar core G335 showed that a binary system, and perhaps even a triple system, could take place below 1000 au (Olguin et al. 2021, 2022).
At present date, it is thus uncertain how will be the multiplicity in the ALMAIMF fields.

referee_caveats_inferred: Core temperatures from PPMAP have a 2.5 arcsec angular resolution (6000-13750 au across 2-5.5 kpc), which is coarser than the 2700 au core extraction resolution, while hot core temperatures are assigned discrete values (100±50 K or 300±100 K) rather than individually fitted values.

Notice that Monte Carlo propagation of temperature, opacity index, and flux uncertainties shifts the MLE power-law exponent systematically from α = 2.11 ± 0.06 to α = 1.97 ± 0.06, which is larger than the quoted 0.02 systematic scatter around the MC mean.

Section 6.3 states that re-introducing massive young stellar objects with free-free emission 'would steepen our CMF even further', whereas adding high-mass cores actually flattens (decreases α of) the high-mass tail of the CMF.
